questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy was recently diagnosed with osteomyelitis due to Serratia marcescens. He has a past medical history of pneumonia due to Nocardia and sepsis due to Burkholderia cepacia.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate screening test?
questions.explanation: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is seen mainly in boys (most common cause is X-linked), and the spectrum of infection is distinct, including Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, and Burkholderia, The DHR test is diagnostic and measures the superoxide production in neutrophils via the NADPH oxidase complex.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q41

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman developed meningococcemia. She had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus and had an episode of meningococcal meningitis at 12 years of age.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate screening test?
questions.explanation: CH50 Recurrent Neisseria infections are a red flag for complement deficiencies, and the past medical history of SLE is another clue toward this diagnosis. The best screening test is CH50. This is a screening test for deficits in either the classic or terminal complement pathways. It tests the functional ability of complement components to lyse antibody-coated sheep red blood cells and is sensitive to a decrease, absence, or inactivity of components in the pathway.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q40

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presented with disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection. He had a past medical history of recurrent nontyphoidal salmonellosis. Investigations: HIV Ag/Ab negative HIV VL not detected
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in the IL-12 or interferon-gamma pathway
A defect in the IL-17 pathway
A defect in the IL-21 pathway

questions.explanation: A defect in the IL-12 or interferon-gamma pathway Inherited defects of innate immunity of the IL-12 or IFNgamma pathways present with disseminated mycobacterial and Salmonella infections. In countries where Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination against tuberculosis is recommended, a common presentation of this disorder is disseminated BCG infection. Defects in the IL-17 pathway lead to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, while defects in the IL-21 pathway lead to hepatobiliary cryptosporidiosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q41

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presented with a third episode of recurrent cough along with a large amount of purulent sputum production. She was known to have common variable immunodeficiency and had multiple episodes of upper and lower respiratory infections. She was afebrile. Investigations: Chest X-ray: parallel linear opacities and a few ring-like shadows
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is an abnormal permanent dilation of the bronchi, typically on the basis of chronic destruction and inflammation caused by recurrent infections or other chronic diseases. Immune deficiencies, such as common variable immunodeficiency and cystic fibrosis, can lead to dilated bronchi. This disorder can lead to purulent sputum production and recurrent cough as well as hemoptysis. The chest imaging findings can demonstrate cystic spaces caused by bronchiectasis or the parallel linear opacities or rings as in this vignette.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q14

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man had a history of frequent skin and upper respiratory bacterial infections. Physical exam revealed silvery hair and findings consistent with Parkinsonism. Investigations: Peripheral blood smear: giant granulocyte inclusions
questions.explanation: Chediak–Higashi syndrome Although both Chediak–Higashi syndrome and Griscelli syndrome can present with silvery hair, immunodeficiency, and neurologic involvement, only Chediak–Higashi syndrome presents with giant inclusions in polymorphonuclear cells.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q42

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman was seen with recurrent skin abscesses since childhood, not accompanied by surrounding redness, warmth, or tenderness. She had also had three episodes of pneumonia, which healed, leaving air-filled cavities. On physical examination she had joint hypermobility, scoliosis, and a wide nasal base. Investigations: Absolute eosinophil count 3000/μL
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyper IgE syndrome Autosomal dominant hyper IgE syndrome manifests with recurrent skin abscesses and recurrent respiratory infections healing with pneumatoceles, as well as eczema and eosinophilia. Nonimmune manifestations include joint laxity, scoliosis, fractures, and a wide nasal tip. DOCK8 deficiency is also associated with hyper IgE and frequent infections but not with skeletal manifestations. Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome also has eczema but is X-linked and is thus mainly seen in males.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q43

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man was diagnosed with disseminated Mycobacterium kansasii infection. On examination, he had multiple warts and bilateral lymphedema of the lower extremities. Investigations: Absolute monocyte count 30/μL
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in innate immunity due to IL-12 or IFNgamma deficiency

questions.explanation: GATA2 deficiency Although patients with deficiencies of the IL-12 and IFNgamma axis and with CGD can present with disseminated mycobacterial infections, while patients with WHIM syndrome (CXCR4 deficiency) and DOCK8 deficiency can present with disseminated warts, patients with GATA2 deficiency also have monocytopenia and lymphedema.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q26

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man was diagnosed with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) after recurrent infections from the age of 5 years old. Hypoparathyroidism was diagnosed after an episode of tetanic spasms at 10 years old. At 15 years of age, he developed adrenal insufficiency.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in the IL-17 axis

questions.explanation: APECED syndrome Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy–Candidiasis–Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED) or autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 is characterized by the triad of CMC, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease. CARD9 deficiency and IL-17 deficiencies can also present with CMC but lack the endocrinopathies. Patients with MCM4 deficiency, on the other hand, also present with adrenal insufficiency, while patients with DiGeorge syndrome also have hypoparathyroidism.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q26

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of headache, nausea, vomiting, neck pain, and low-grade fever. He underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for alcoholic cirrhosis 6 months prior and was on high-dose steroids for induction and tacrolimus and mycophenolate for maintenance immunosuppression. He was on secondary prophylaxis with valganciclovir for CMV syndrome. MRI brain: multiple rim-enhancing lesions along the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, corpus callosum, and cerebellum.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Perform a brain biopsy The differential for this presentation is too broad, and empiricism may lead to bad outcomes. The patient underwent a stereotactic needle biopsy of the right frontal lesion. Pathology showed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that was CD20-positive. In situ hybridization was positive for EBVencoded small RNA (EBER). A PET scan showed no activity outside of the CNS. This was a case of posttransplant primary CNS lymphoma, which carries a dismal prognosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q24

questions.stem: A toddler presented with Pneumocystic jirovecii pneumonia, following a long-standing history of diarrhea, failure to thrive, and developmental delay. Laboratory examination revealed macrocytic anemia, leucopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils, and thrombocytopenia, as well as hypogammaglobulinemia.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hereditary folate malabsorption All these conditions can present with pneumocystis pneumonia. Cartilage–hair hypoplasia can also present with macrocytic anemia and short stature, but it lacks the other features of the disease (in particular, diarrhea and neurologic involvement). CD40L deficiency is accompanied by elevated IgM concentrations, while SP110 deficiency exhibits hepatic veno-occlusive disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q27

questions.model_answer:
Chronic granulomatous disease (example): Phagocytes - defective NADPH oxidase prevents neutrophils from generating the oxidative (respiratory) burst needed to kill catalase-positive organisms.
Properdin deficiency: Complement - properdin stabilizes the alternative-pathway C3 convertase; deficiency (X-linked) impairs the alternative complement pathway, causing susceptibility to Neisseria meningitidis.
DiGeorge syndrome: T cell (cellular) - thymic hypoplasia/aplasia (22q11 deletion) impairs T-cell development and number.
Common variable immunodeficiency: B cell (humoral) - defective B-cell differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells with impaired immunoglobulin production (low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM).
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter grounds the humoral/B-cell and complement/properdin arms (p. 3619) but not the specific PID mechanisms (DiGeorge thymic hypoplasia, CVID differentiation defect), which come from immunology references.

cohort_answer.text: CGD (example): Phagocytes - Deficiency in NADPH oxidase prevents neutrophils from generating an oxidative burst. Properdin deficiency: Complement - Properdin is an early component of the alternative pathway; deficiency causes impaired alternative pathway and susceptibility to meningococcal infections (X-linked, seen in males). Di George Syndrome: T cell (+B cell) - Thymic hypoplasia causing impaired T cell numbers/function, also B cell defects. CVID: B cell - Defective B cell differentiation into plasma cells, impaired Ig secretion; Low IgG, low/normal IgM and A, normal IgE.

questions.model_answer:
a) X-linked recessive (defect in CYBB/gp91phox) - the most common, roughly two-thirds of cases; and autosomal recessive (the remaining genotypes).
b) A defect in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, so neutrophils and macrophages cannot generate the respiratory (oxidative) burst and reactive oxygen species, and fail to kill ingested catalase-positive organisms.
c) Skin: granulomatous lesions, poor wound healing, pyoderma. GI tract: granulomatous inflammation mimicking inflammatory bowel disease/colitis, and obstruction (e.g., gastric outlet).
d) (1) Staphylococcus aureus (2) Aspergillus spp. (3) Burkholderia cepacia complex (4) Serratia marcescens (also Nocardia spp.).
e) (1) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole antibacterial prophylaxis (2) Itraconazole antifungal prophylaxis (3) Interferon-gamma immunomodulatory prophylaxis (avoid BCG and live bacterial vaccines).
questions.beyond_mandell: CGD inheritance, pathophysiology, pathogens, and prophylaxis from established immunology (Mandell primary immunodeficiency chapter); not covered in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Inheritance: X-linked - more common, ~65%; Autosomal recessive (4 types, all less common than X-linked). Pathophysiology: Defect in NADPH oxidase complex, preventing phagocytes from destroying ingested organisms. Non-infectious manifestations - Skin: poor wound healing, pyoderma gangrenosum, granulomatous acne, inflammatory nodular lesions, photosensitivity. GI tract: granulomatous GI inflammation (can mimic IBD/colitis), weight loss/FTT, rarely obstruction from large granulomas. Other manifestations: pulmonary granulomas, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (mulch pneumonitis), rheumatologic (SLE, RA, IgA nephropathy), GU (strictures), ocular (chorioretinitis). Most common pathogens: Aspergillus species (2.6/100 patient-years); S. aureus (1.44/100 patient-years); Burkholderia cepacia complex (1.06/100 patient-years); Serratia marcescens (0.98/100 patient-years); Nocardia species (0.81/100 patient-years). Prevention: Genetic testing before having kids; Antimicrobial prophylaxis (TMP-SMX, Antifungal: Itraconazole, Immunomodulatory: IFN-gamma); Vaccination (BCG contraindicated, live bacterial vaccines avoided e.g. Salmonella, live viral vaccines recommended - not affected by CGD)

questions.model_answer: a) CGD: Impairment = phagocyte defect in NADPH oxidase, failure of the respiratory (oxidative) burst so ingested catalase-positive organisms are not killed; Vulnerability = catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, Burkholderia cepacia complex, Nocardia, Aspergillus) causing recurrent pneumonia, abscesses (liver, perianal), suppurative adenitis, osteomyelitis; Diagnosis = dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry or neutrophil oxidative burst/NBT test; Prophylaxis = lifelong TMP-SMX plus itraconazole (+/- interferon-gamma). Properdin deficiency: Impairment = X-linked deficiency of the alternative-complement-pathway stabiliser properdin, impaired opsonisation/membrane-attack complex formation; Vulnerability = fulminant Neisseria meningitidis (and gonococcal) disease; Diagnosis = AH50 (alternative pathway) assay, properdin level; Prophylaxis = meningococcal vaccination (ACWY conjugate and serogroup B). CVID: Impairment = humoral defect with normal/near-normal B-cell numbers but failure of differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells; Vulnerability = recurrent sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae), bronchiectasis, GI infection/enteropathy (Giardia, norovirus, Campylobacter); Diagnosis = low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM, poor vaccine (polysaccharide/protein) responses, exclusion of secondary causes; Prophylaxis = immunoglobulin replacement (IVIG/SCIG). DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion): Impairment = thymic hypoplasia/aplasia causing T-cell (cellular) deficiency, variable severity; Vulnerability = viral, fungal and opportunistic infections in complete DiGeorge (SCID-like phenotype); milder forms have recurrent sinopulmonary infection; Diagnosis = low T-cell count/CD3 count, FISH or microarray for 22q11.2 deletion; Prophylaxis = none for partial forms; complete DiGeorge needs PCP prophylaxis, irradiated/CMV-negative blood, and thymic or stem-cell transplant.
questions.beyond_mandell: This general-principles chapter (Ch. 305) does not tabulate the primary immunodeficiencies; content drawn from Mandell primary-immunodeficiency chapters and standard immunology/PID references.

cohort_answer.text: CGD: Phagocyte deficiency, impaired NADPH oxidase complex function; vulnerable to catalase positive organisms (S. aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia complex, Nocardia, Aspergillus), recurrent PNA, abscesses, suppurative adenitis, bacteremias, SSTI; diagnosis NOBT (neutrophil oxidase burst test); prophylaxis lifelong Septra + Itraconazole. Properdin deficiency: complement factor deficiency in alternate pathway, only affects males; vulnerable to Neisseria infections (severe meningococcal disease, gonorrhea); diagnosis AH50 assay (can be normal); prophylaxis vaccination with Menactra (ACWY) and Bexsero (B). CVID: humoral deficiency (sufficient B cells but impaired antibody production); recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic lung disease, GI disease (IBD); diagnosis reduced total IgG, reduced IgA/IgM, poor response to immunization, no other immunodeficiency; prophylaxis IVIG. DiGeorge: cellular deficiency, thymic hypoplasia reduces T cell numbers (some also SCID phenotype, IgA deficiency, hypogammaglobulinemia, or SAD); recurrent URTIs, SCID phenotype develops recurrent sinopulmonary infections and chronic diarrhea; diagnosis genetic testing, FISH, microarray; prophylaxis none unless SCID phenotype (then PCP ppx +/- IVIG).

questions.model_answer: a) They are biologics that neutralise TNF-alpha: monoclonal antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab) and the soluble receptor fusion protein etanercept. They bind and neutralise soluble/membrane TNF, dampening the proinflammatory cascade; the monoclonal antibodies also induce apoptosis/complement lysis of TNF-expressing cells, giving them higher granulomatous-infection risk than etanercept. b) TNF-alpha is a key proinflammatory cytokine required for macrophage activation, recruitment of inflammatory cells, and granuloma formation/maintenance that contains intracellular pathogens; its inhibition predisposes to organisms normally sequestered in granulomas. c) Most common/characteristic: reactivation tuberculosis. Four others: (1) dimorphic fungi (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis); (2) hepatitis B reactivation; (3) Listeria monocytogenes; (4) Legionella (also Cryptococcus, PJP).
questions.beyond_mandell: TNF-inhibitor mechanism and infection spectrum are from Mandell TNF-inhibitor/immunomodulator chapters; Ch. 305 notes only that anticytokine agents raise infection risk (p. 3619).

cohort_answer.text: MOA: Neutralize TNF; modulate cytokine response (reduce inflammation); reduction of pro-inflammatory T-cell subsets (Th1, Th2, Th17); increase in anti-inflammatory helper and regulatory T cells; induces apoptosis of pro-inflammatory immune cells. Natural function: important pro-inflammatory cytokine crucial for formation/activation of macrophages, phagosomes, granulomas; TNF-alpha inhibition predisposes to infection by intracellular pathogens and those usually sequestered into granulomas. Most common infection: TB (classic). Other associated infections: Dimorphic fungi (histo, cocci, blasto); Hepatitis B; Listeria; Legionella; Cryptococcus neoformans; Toxoplasmosis.

questions.model_answer:
a) TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab, and the soluble receptor etanercept) bind and neutralize both soluble and membrane-bound TNF-alpha, preventing its interaction with the TNFR1/TNFR2 receptors. This blocks the downstream pro-inflammatory cascade (reduced IL-1, IL-6, chemokine release and leukocyte/endothelial activation) and impairs formation and maintenance of granulomas; the monoclonal antibodies (unlike etanercept) also bind membrane TNF and can induce complement- and antibody-dependent lysis and apoptosis of TNF-expressing inflammatory cells.
b) (1) Rheumatoid arthritis; (2) Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease / ulcerative colitis); (3) Ankylosing spondylitis (also psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis, hidradenitis suppurativa).
c) (1) Reactivation of latent tuberculosis (and non-tuberculous mycobacteria) due to loss of granuloma integrity; (2) Endemic/dimorphic fungi - histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis (and other opportunists e.g. Pneumocystis, invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis); (3) Intracellular bacteria - Listeria monocytogenes, Legionella; (4) Reactivation of hepatitis B; other reported associations include cryptococcosis, toxoplasmosis, and crusted (Norwegian) scabies.
questions.beyond_mandell: The detailed receptor-level mechanism, the specific list of licensed indications, and the classic TB/endemic-fungi/Listeria/Legionella/HBV reactivation risks are drawn from established knowledge (Mandell agent-specific chapters and product/IDSA guidance); this General Principles chapter references only anti-cytokine antibody infection risk (p. 3619) and a Norwegian scabies outbreak under TNF-alpha inhibitors (p. 3624).

questions.model_answer:
a) Rituximab: chimeric monoclonal Ab targeting CD20 on pre-B and mature B cells causing B-cell lysis/depletion (B-cell malignancies, autoimmune disease). Characteristic risk: HBV reactivation (may be fatal; screen HBsAg/HBcAb) and PML.
b) Tocilizumab: monoclonal Ab against IL-6/IL-6 receptor (binds soluble and membrane-bound IL-6), used in RA, GCA, JIA. Risks: TB and other mycobacteria, disseminated fungi (candidiasis, aspergillosis, cryptococcosis, PJP), herpes zoster.
c) Ustekinumab: monoclonal Ab against the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23 (psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn). Risks: mycobacterial/BCG/Salmonella infection (IL-12/23 axis), Listeria meningitis, HSV; TB reactivation reported.
d) Belimumab: monoclonal Ab against B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS/BAFF), inhibiting B-cell survival and differentiation into plasma cells (SLE). Risks: fatal CMV pneumonia, PML.
e) Abatacept: CTLA-4-Ig fusion protein binding CD80/CD86 on APCs, blocking CD28 T-cell costimulation (RA, JIA, PsA). Risks: pneumonia/sepsis; rare TB reactivation; HBV reactivation (screen).
f) Belatacept: higher-avidity CTLA-4-Ig blocking CD28 costimulation, used for rejection prophylaxis in renal transplantation. Characteristic risk: EBV-associated PTLD (especially CNS, in EBV-seronegative recipients); increased CMV disease.
g) Natalizumab: monoclonal Ab against the alpha-4 integrin subunit, blocking leukocyte adhesion/migration into tissue (relapsing MS, Crohn). Hallmark risk: PML (JCV) — risk rises with anti-JCV Ab positivity, >2 yr use, and prior immunosuppression.
h) Fingolimod: sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator sequestering lymphocytes in lymph nodes (relapsing MS). Risks: disseminated/fatal HSV and VZV, cryptococcosis (including meningitis), PML/JCV, atypical mycobacteria.
i) Anti-TNF: monoclonal Abs or soluble TNF receptor binding TNF-alpha (RA, IBD, psoriasis). Classic risk: reactivation TB; also granulomatous/intracellular infections (histoplasmosis, Listeria, Legionella) and HBV reactivation.
j) Eculizumab: monoclonal Ab binding C5, preventing C5a/C5b and blocking terminal complement/MAC (PNH, aHUS, myasthenia gravis). Characteristic risk: life-threatening Neisseria meningitidis (even in vaccinated patients); encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib) in children.
k) IL-5 inhibitors (mepolizumab, reslizumab): monoclonal Abs against IL-5, reducing eosinophil differentiation/survival (severe eosinophilic asthma). Risks: herpes zoster (mepolizumab); unmasking of helminth/Strongyloides infection (treat before therapy).
questions.beyond_mandell: Belatacept (renal-transplant rejection prophylaxis; EBV-PTLD, CMV) and the detailed anti-TNF infection profile (TB reactivation, histoplasmosis/Listeria/Legionella) are not in this slice; drawn from established Mandell/product-monograph knowledge.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort lists belatacept as a treatment for RA/JIA, but belatacept is used for renal-transplant rejection prophylaxis (abatacept, not belatacept, is the RA/JIA agent); its EBV-associated PTLD risk is correct.

cohort_answer.text:
Rituximab – chimeric antibody to CD-20 monoclonal antibody causing B cell depletion. Used in B cell malignancies and autoimmune d/o. Associated with HBV reactivation.
Tocilizumab – monoclonal antibody to IL-6 receptor used to treat RA/JIA. Associated with Herpes Zoster, PJP and atypical mycobacterial infection, crypto.
Ustekinumab (stelara) – monoclonal antibody to IL-12 and IL-23 to treat plaque psoriasis. Nothing specific.
Belimumab – monoclonal antibody to B lymphocyte stimulator protein that inhibits B cell survival and therefore inhibits differentiation into Ig plasma cells. Used to treat SLE. Cocci and CMV pneumonia reported.
Abatacept – CTLA-4 Ig blocks CD28 T cell costimulation, used to treat RA. No specific infections risks identified.
Belatacept – CTLA-4 IG blocks CD28 costimulation. Used in RA and JIA. No particular infection risk. Associated with PTLD.
Natalizumab – inhibits migration of leukocytes, used to treat MS, Crohn's, plaque psoriasis. Associated with PML. Withdrawn from Canadian market
Fingolimod – prevents lymphocyte movement out of lymph nodes, used to treat MS. Associated with life threatening herpes virus infections.
Anti-TNF – antibodies to TNF or soluble TNF receptor that binds TNF, used to treat RA, IBD etc. Associated with TB.
Eculizumab – monoclonal ab that binds C5 and inhibits terminal compliment activation. Increased risk of Neisseria infections.
IL-5 inhibitor (mepolizumab, reslizumab) - Risk for herpes zoster, strongyloides.
